name: expiry_wings_v1
question: the expiry-eve strangle earns most of its money on ordinary days and gives most of it back on a handful of shock days (2% of BANKNIFTY trades lost Rs 2.06L of its Rs 3.52L total). Can far wings, bought as crash insurance, cap that tail while keeping most of the edge?
data: NSE F&O bhavcopy 2019-01 to the latest warehouse release (runtime/warehouse fo_bhav_*.parquet), evidence class real_eod_approximation; the same conventions as warehouse_research.build_trades: entry at the close one session before expiry, legs at close -/+ leg_cost, statutory fees, held to the expiry-day close, STT on exercised long legs; only strikes that traded that day
trials: 3 new candidates on top of the 40 configurations of the original study; reported with every result

account.sizing: lots = floor(Rs 20,000 / the median max loss per lot); the naked reference is sized by its 1st-percentile loss for comparison only

reported: per index and variant: n, mean, sd, t, win rate, worst, 1st percentile, CVaR 5% (mean of the worst 5%), median max loss per lot, credit kept vs the strangle, mean in the first two thirds and the last third, P&L by year, lots under the budget and expected rupees a year at Rs 5L
selection: per index, a candidate qualifies when its full-sample t >= 2 and its mean is positive in both the first two thirds and the last third. Among qualifiers, the one with the highest expected rupees a year at Rs 5L under the loss budget is selected. With no qualifier, sleeve A stays as registered
use: the selection becomes sleeve C in a new forward spec (expiry_seller_v2) on real quotes, exactly like v1; nothing here goes live or changes v1
changes: evaluated once; a different wing rule is a new spec
